title: Josephson energy of superconducting junctions: amorphous versus crystalline tunnel barriers
authors: Wanting Zhang, Aldilene Saraiva-Souza, Félix Beaudoin, Xianghua Kong, Hong Guo, Yu Zhu
abstract: The Josephson energy $E_J$ is a key parameter governing the properties of transmon superconducting qubits. In Al/AlO$_x$/Al junctions, $E_J$ is set by electron tunneling through an ultrathin oxide barrier and therefore depends exponentially on the atomic structure of the barrier. We compute $E_J$ by first-principles device modeling based on the NEGF-DFT quantum-transport method, comparing a junction with a crystalline Al$_2$O$_3$ barrier against ten junctions with melt--quenched amorphous Al$_2$O$_3$ barriers of the same thickness. From the Fermi-level transmission and the Ambegaokar--Baratoff relation, we obtain a mean $E_J/h$ of $2.78$ GHz for the amorphous ensemble, with a standard deviation of $4.67$ GHz, compared with $0.73$ GHz for the crystalline reference; individual amorphous values span nearly two orders of magnitude. Scattering-state analysis shows that transport is quantum tunneling and that the variability originates from stoichiometric inhomogeneity of the amorphous oxide: Al-rich, low-barrier regions can connect into percolation-like tunneling pathways that strongly enhance the conductance. A realistic $200\times200$ nm$^2$ junction self-averages over more than $2\times10^4$ such microscopic regions. These results establish a quantitative atomistic route from oxide microstructure to the superconducting-circuit energy scale $E_J$.
summary: This theoretical study quantifies the Josephson energy in superconducting junctions by comparing crystalline and amorphous oxide barriers. Using NEGF-DFT, the authors find that amorphous barriers show high variability and a higher mean $E_J$ due to percolation pathways. This work provides a crucial atomistic understanding of how oxide disorder dictates superconducting circuit performance.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the atomic structure of the tunnel barrier affects the Josephson energy ($E_J$) in superconducting junctions, a critical parameter for transmon qubits.
main_result: Amorphous barriers exhibit a significantly higher mean $E_J$ compared to crystalline barriers, with variability arising from percolation-like tunneling paths due to stoichiometric inhomogeneity.
method: The Josephson energy is calculated using first-principles quantum transport modeling based on the NEGF-DFT method, combined with the Ambegaokar–Baratoff relation.
model_or_system: The system is an Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junction, modeled using the Hamiltonian relevant to transmon qubits. The comparison is made between a perfectly crystalline $	ext{Al}_2	ext{O}_3$ barrier and multiple realizations of melt-quenched amorphous $	ext{Al}_2	ext{O}_3$ barriers.
key_observables: Josephson energy ($E_J$), normal-state conductance ($G_{A/N}$), and the transmission coefficient $T(E)$.
important_parameters: The superconducting gap ($\Delta$), the junction area ($200 	imes 200 	ext{ nm}^2$), and the ratio $E_J/h$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the superconducting properties are governed by the Ambegaokar–Baratoff relation and that the transport mechanism is quantum tunneling.
figures_summary: Figures compare the atomic structures of crystalline versus amorphous barriers, show the calculated $E_J$ values for multiple amorphous samples against the crystalline reference, and visualize the probability of Fermi-level scattering states.
paper_structure: The paper follows a computational workflow: first, calculating the transmission coefficient $T(E)$ via NEGF-DFT; second, determining the critical current $I_c$ via the Ambegaokar–Baratoff relation; and finally, calculating $E_J$ for both crystalline and various amorphous barrier structures.
why_interesting: The direct link established between the nanoscale, disordered microstructure (amorphous oxide) and a macroscopic circuit parameter ($E_J$) is highly relevant for designing reliable quantum hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Atomic structures of the Josephson-junction models. (a) Junction with a crystalline Al2O3 tunnel barrier. (b) Junction with an amorphous Al2O3 tunnel barrier of the same oxide thickness. Blue and red spheres represent Al and O atoms, respectively.

Figure 2: Josephson energies of the ten amorphous junction samples (bars), estimated from the calculated Fermi-level transmission using the Ambegaokar–Baratoff relation with ∆= 0.18 meV and a device area of 200 × 200 nm2. Each junction is scaled using its corresponding transverse simulation-cell area A0. The dashed line marks the crystalline reference junction (EJ/h ≈0.73 GHz).

Figure 3: Area-normalized energy-dependent transmission T(E)/A0 on a logarithmic scale, where A0 is the transverse area of the corresponding simulation cell. The thick black curve is the crystalline junction; the colored curves are the ten amorphous junctions. Normalization by A0 accounts for the different transverse supercell areas of the crystalline and amorphous models. All curves exhibit a similar transmission-valley structure, while their values near the Fermi level vary substantially among samples.

Figure 4: Probability of the Fermi-level scattering states (natural-log scale), averaged over the transverse xy dimensions, for all 64 transport channels in each of the ten amorphous junction samples. The panels correspond to Samples 1–10, and the color denotes the transport-channel index. The approximately linear decay within the oxide on the logarithmic scale is characteristic of quantum tunneling; the different decay rates show that some channels are considerably more conductive than others.

Figure 5 visualizes two representative scattering states in real space: (a) the least conductive channel of Sample 5, the lowest-transmission junction, and (b) the most conductive channel of Sample 6, the highest-transmission junction. In the least conductive case, the wave function remains confined to the incident electrode and interface region and dies out inside the oxide; in the most conductive case, it penetrates the barrier and retains substantial amplitude on the transmitted side. These observations suggest the following physical picture.
